PROGRAM DESCRIPTION 
 
The Bachelor of Science in Information Technology (BSIT) program is a 
four-year degree program which focuses on the study of computer utilization and 
computer software to plan, install, customize, operate, manage, administer and 
maintain information technology infrastructure. It likewise deals with the design 
and development of computer-based information systems for real-world business 
solutions. 
 
The program prepares students to become IT professionals with primary 
competencies in the areas of systems analysis and design, applications 
development, database administration, network administration, and systems 
implementation and maintenance. 
The program also requires a Capstone project. It should be in the form of an IT 
applications development as a business solution for an industry need. 
 
 
COURSE DESCRIPTION 
 
This course unit offers an introduction to the latest, cutting-edge research 
outcomes in the area of database management systems (DBMSs). It starts with 
a brief overview of the internal architecture of traditional DBMSs, and proceeds 
to cover a range of advanced systems that extend that architecture to different 
execution environments than the classical, centralized one. The viewpoint 
adopted throughout is systems-oriented and research-oriented. Focus falls on 
the impacts on classical query processing functionality (i.e., impacts on other 
DBMS-provided services such as storage, concurrency and transaction 
management are largely ignored) with the use of Adv. SQL. 
 
 
This course discusses database system implementation techniques such 
as concurrency control, transaction processing, scheduling, and recovery. It also 
covers discussions on the current trends in database systems in different

based database systems and emerging database applications and technologies.

Preface 
 
 
This instructional material (IM) is designed to provide students with a 
comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of data structures and 
algorithms. It is intended for students who have a basic understanding of 
programming and are eager to explore the world of efficient data organization 
and manipulation.

specific data structure or algorithmic concept. The topics covered include arrays, 
linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, balanced trees, graphs, hashing, and file 
structures. Each unit presents the theoretical foundations of the topic, followed 
by practical examples and exercises to reinforce understanding. 
The IM emphasizes the importance of algorithm analysis, enabling students to 
evaluate the efficiency of different algorithms and choose the most suitable one 
for a given task. It also highlights the trade-offs between different data structures 
and algorithms, encouraging students to consider factors such as time 
complexity, space complexity, and ease of implementation when making design 
decisions. 
 
Throughout the IM, students are encouraged to actively engage with the 
material through various learning activities, including coding exercises, review 
questions, and case studies. By applying the concepts they learn to practical 
problems, students will develop the skills necessary to design and implement 
efficient data structures and algorithms in their own programs. 
 
We hope that this IM will serve as a valuable resource for students 
embarking on their journey into the fascinating world of data structures and 
algorithms. By mastering these concepts, students will be well-equipped to 
tackle complex programming challenges and develop innovative solutions in 
their future careers.

What is a Database? 
 
A database is an organized collection of related data which represents some aspect of 
the real world and that is stored and accessed electronically. Databases are designed to 
efficiently manage large amounts of information by providing a systematic way to store, 
retrieve, and manipulate data. They are used in various applications, ranging from simple 
personal data management to complex enterprise systems (Joe, C. 2021). 
 
In the changing world of a database, tables are the fundamental structures that

arrangement of records offered in rows and columns. It improves the performance of

DBMS Definition and its Key Functions 
 
Database Management Systems (DBMS) is a software system used to store, retrieve, 
and run queries on data. It provides a systematic and organized way of storing, managing, 
and retrieving data, ensuring data integrity, security, and consistency. A DBMS serves as an 
interface between an end-user and a database, allowing users to create, read, update, and 
delete data in the database. 
 
DBMS manage the data, the database engine, and the database schema, allowing for 
data to be manipulated or extracted by users and other programs. This helps provide data 
security, data integrity, concurrency, and uniform data administration procedures. DBMS 
optimizes the organization of data by following a database schema design technique called 
normalization, which splits a large table into smaller tables when any of its attributes have 
redundancy in values. 
 
DBMS offer many benefits over traditional file systems, including flexibility and a more 
complex backup system. Database management systems can be classified based on a 
variety of criteria such as the data model, the database distribution, or user numbers. The 
most widely used types of DBMS software are relational, distributed, hierarchical, object-
oriented, and network. Here’s an in-depth look at what DBMS entails (Friedrichsen, Lisa et 
al. 2021):

1. Data Definition 
• Schema Definition: Defines the database structure, including tables, fields, 
relationships, and constraints. 
• Data Types: Specifies the types of data that can be stored (e.g., integers, strings, 
dates). 
2. Data Manipulation 
• Query Processing: Allows users to retrieve specific data using query languages like 
SQL. 
• Data Update: Enables insertion, modification, and deletion of data within the 
database. 
• Transaction Management: Ensures that transactions are processed reliably and 
adhere to ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). 
3. Data Security and Integrity 
• Access Control: Manages user permissions to ensure only authorized users can 
access or modify data. 
• Integrity Constraints: Enforces rules to maintain data accuracy and consistency (e.g., 
primary keys, foreign keys). 
4. Data Storage and Retrieval 
• Storage Management: Handles the physical storage of data on disk drives. 
• Indexing: Creates indexes to speed up data retrieval operations. 
• Backup and Recovery: Provides mechanisms to back up data and restore it in case 
of data loss or corruption. 
5. Data Administration 
• Database Tuning: Optimizes database performance through techniques like 
indexing and query optimization. 
• Monitoring and Maintenance: Tracks database performance and performs regular 
maintenance tasks.

Types of DBMS 
1. Relational DBMS (RDBMS) 
The concept of a relational database is elaborated as a pivotal development in data 
management, pioneered by Edgar Frank Codd from IBM. The commercial adoption of 
relational databases began approximately a decade after Codd's initial work, significantly 
marked by the creation of Oracle. This advancement allowed for modifications in database 
structures without necessitating changes in the design of applications relying on the 
database, thereby enhancing flexibility and adaptability. Relational databases organize data 
into separate tables, known as relations, where each table consists of rows and columns. 
Each row is unique, and each cell contains a single value, ensuring data integrity and 
atomicity. This modular structure allows for independent changes in one table without 
adversely affecting others, simplifying data management and maintenance. The relational 
model's ability to provide efficient data storage, retrieval, and manipulation has made it a

dominant standard in database systems, promoting consistency, scalability, and ease of use 
in managing complex datasets (Joe, C. 2021). 
We should dissect this construction in more detail: 
a. Schema: This is basically the actual design, otherwise called the theoretical view or 
legitimate view. It is likewise the part of the data set which addresses the metadata. 
As you definitely know, metadata is the thing that furnishes us with the data about 
the information base. It depicts the design, the tables, and all that is put away inside 
them. In this manner, you can say that metadata is truth be told information all alone. 
b. Domain: Each table segment has a trait that includes various qualities. The 
assortment of these qualities addresses the space of that trait. For example, suppose 
you have an information base that contains various distinctive vehicle models. The 
tables for these vehicles will incorporate a section called "shading". Presently 
suppose there's a Nissan Qashqai which comes in a few unique tones like metallic 
silver, dark, pearl white, and cherry red. These tones together address the shading 
property's area. 
c. Constraints: They are pretty much as significant as the wide range of various 
segments, anyway they are frequently undervalued and overlooked, particularly by 
the individuals who simply begin in the specialized universe of information bases. As 
the name proposes, an information base's imperatives characterize which esteems 
can have a place with quality. The essential capacity of a requirement is to restrict 
different clients from presenting some unacceptable data in the table. Remember 
that these qualities that do have a place with a specific area should likewise consent

resembles applying unbending limitations. This implies that the area of a segment is 
indeed decided by the actual qualities as well as by the limitations too. 
• Structure: Uses tables (relations) to store data, with rows representing records and 
columns representing fields. 
• Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server.

21 
 
• Key Feature: SQL (Structured Query Language) for querying and managing data. 
 
2. NoSQL DBMS 
 
NoSQL, which stands for "Not Only SQL," refers to a category of database management 
systems that diverge from the traditional relational database management system (RDBMS) 
approach. NoSQL databases are designed to handle large volumes of data, diverse data types, 
and dynamic schema requirements, which are increasingly common in modern applications. 
They provide flexible data models and are optimized for performance, scalability, and 
horizontal expansion (Friedrichsen, Lisa et al. 2021). 
• Structure: Designed for unstructured or semi-structured data, offering flexible schema 
models. 
Types: 
• Document-Oriented: Stores data as documents (e.g., MongoDB, CouchDB). 
• Key-Value Stores: Stores data as key-value pairs (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB). 
• Column-Family Stores: Stores data in columns rather than rows (e.g., Cassandra, 
HBase). 
• Graph Databases: Focuses on data relationships using graph structures (e.g., Neo4j, 
ArangoDB). 
• Key Feature: Scalability and flexibility for handling big data and complex data types. 
 
3. Object-Oriented DBMS (OODBMS) 
 
An Object-Oriented Database Management System (OODBMS) is a type of database 
management system that supports the creation and modeling of data as objects. This 
approach is designed to integrate with object-oriented programming (OOP) languages with 
database technology, enabling developers to store data in a format that closely resembles 
their application's objects. It allows for the storage of complex data structures and supports

22 
 
advanced features like inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism. OODBMS was created 
to take advantage of object-oriented programming concepts but faced challenges in 
becoming widely adopted due to compatibility issues with traditional relational databases (Joe, 
C. 2021). 
• Structure: Stores data as objects, similar to object-oriented programming. 
• Examples: ObjectDB, db4o. 
• Key Feature: Integration with object-oriented programming languages. 
 
4. Hierarchical and Network DBMS 
 
Hierarchical and Network Database Management Systems (DBMS) both emerged in 
the early days of database technology, offering structured ways to manage data with distinct 
approaches. Hierarchical DBMS organizes data in a tree-like structure where each record 
(node) has a single parent and multiple children, resembling an organizational chart. This rigid 
structure ensures simplicity and efficient data retrieval for hierarchical queries but is less 
flexible for complex relationships. Network DBMS, on the other hand, extends the hierarchical 
model by allowing multiple parent-child relationships, forming a graph-like structure. This 
flexibility supports more complex data relationships and efficient querying but at the cost of 
increased complexity in design and maintenance. Both systems use pointers to navigate 
between records and ensure data integrity through well-defined relationships.  
 
However, Hierarchical DBMS is simpler and more straightforward to implement, while 
Network DBMS offers greater flexibility and efficiency for complex, interconnected data 
scenarios (Friedrichsen, Lisa et al. 2021).

Lesson 4: Advantages of Using a DBMS 
 
Understanding the advantages of using a DBMS is crucial for anyone involved in data-
centric roles or organizations. Using a Database Management System (DBMS) offers several 
advantages that enhance data management, security, efficiency, and scalability. Here are 
the key advantages (Friedrichsen, Lisa et al. 2021): 
1. Centralized Data Management: 
 
A DBMS allows for centralized storage of data, which means all data is stored in one 
place rather than scattered across various files or systems. 
• Simplifies data access and retrieval. 
• Reduces data redundancy and inconsistency. 
• Facilitates easier data backup and recovery.

24 
 
2. Improved Data Security: 
 
DBMS provides built-in security measures to protect data from unauthorized access 
and ensure data integrity. 
• Implements access control mechanisms. 
• Offers encryption capabilities for sensitive data. 
• Maintains audit trails for accountability. 
 
3. Efficient Data Retrieval and Manipulation: 
DBMS provides powerful query languages and indexing techniques to retrieve and 
manipulate data quickly and efficiently. 
• Supports complex queries and ad-hoc reporting. 
• Optimizes data access through indexing. 
• Enhances performance for data-intensive applications. 
 
4. Data Consistency and Integrity: 
DBMS enforces data integrity constraints to ensure that data entered into the database is 
accurate and consistent. 
• Enforces rules and relationships among data entities. 
• Prevents data anomalies and inconsistencies. 
• Maintains data quality and reliability. 
 
5. Scalability and Flexibility: 
DBMS supports scalability by handling increasing amounts of data and users without 
sacrificing performance.

UNDERSTANDING TO JOINS WITH MYSQL 
 
   Introduction                            
 
In relational databases, data is often spread across multiple tables to minimize 
redundancy and maintain data integrity. However, retrieving meaningful insights often 
requires combining data from these separate tables. This is where SQL Joins become 
essential. A SQL Join is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a 
related column between them. MySQL, as one of the most widely used relational 
database management systems, supports several types of joins that allow developers 
and analysts to retrieve integrated views of data. 
In this module, students will explore the concept of SQL joins with a focus on how they 
are implemented in MySQL. Through practical examples and guided practice, students 
will learn to write queries using inner joins, left joins, right joins, and full outer joins. 
These join types help users navigate complex datasets and make meaningful 
connections between tables, supporting more powerful data retrieval and analysis (Edet, 
T., 2024). 
    Learning Outcomes 
At the end of this lesson, the student should be able to: 
1. Explain the concept and importance of SQL joins in relational databases. 
2. Apply INNER JOIN to retrieve matching data from two or more tables. 
3. Use LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN to retrieve data from one table even when there is no match 
in the other. 
4. Understand and utilize FULL OUTER JOIN (using MySQL-compatible methods) to retrieve 
all records when there is a match in either table.

Lesson 1. Inner Join Clause 
 
The INNER JOIN matches each row in one table with every row in other tables and 
allows you to query rows that contain columns from both tables. 
The INNER JOIN is an optional clause of the SELECT statement. It appears immediately 
after the FROM clause. Here is the syntax of the INNER JOIN clause: 
 
In this syntax: 
• First, specify the main table that appears in the FROM clause (t1). 
• Second, specify the table that will be joined with the main table, which appears 
in the INNER JOIN clause (t2, t3,…). 
• Third, specify a join condition after the ON keyword of the INNER JOIN clause. 
The join condition specifies the rule for matching rows between the main table 
and the table appeared in the INNER JOIN clause. 
Assuming that you want to join two tables t1 and t2. 
The following statement illustrates how to join two tables t1 and t2 using the INNER 
JOIN clause:

select_list

...;

select_list 
FROM 
t1 
INNER JOIN t2 ON join_condition;

The INNER JOIN clause compares each row in the t1 table with every row in the t2 
table based on the join condition. 
 
If rows from both tables cause the join condition to evaluate to TRUE, the INNER 
JOIN creates a new row whose columns contain all columns of rows from the tables and 
includes this new row in the result set. Otherwise, the INNER JOIN just ignores the rows. 
 
In case no row between tables causes the join condition to evaluate to TRUE, the 
INNER JOIN returns an empty result set. This logic is also applied when you join more 
than 2 tables.

Lesson 2. MySQL Left Join Clause 
 
 
Similar to an inner join, a left join also requires a join-predicate. When joining two 
tables using a left join, the concepts of left and right tables are introduced. The left join 
selects data starting from the left table. For each row in the left table, the left join compares 
with every row in the right table. If the values in the two rows cause the join condition 
evaluates to true, the left join creates a new row whose columns contain all columns of the 
rows in both tables and includes this row in the result set (MySQL Join Made Easy For 
Beginners, n.d.). 
 
If the values in the two rows are not matched, the left join clause still creates a new 
row whose columns contain columns of the row in the left table and NULL for columns of 
the row in the right table. In other words, the left join selects all data from the left table 
whether there are matching rows exist in the right table or not. In case there is no matching 
rows from the right table found, NULLs are used for columns of the row from the right 
table in the final result set (MySQL Join Made Easy For Beginners, n.d.).
